sections.h2: What a Garfield Heights seller should know first
sections.html:
Garfield Heights puts an inspection between the contract and the closing table. Sellers apply to the Building Department for a Certificate of Inspection, and the city issues a Compliance Certificate that the buyer needs for title transfer.

The city sits in Cuyahoga County, borders Cleveland, covers 7.23 square miles of land, and uses ZIP codes 44105, 44125 and 44128. Home values are low by regional standards: the median owner-occupied home is $109,900, and 58.5 percent of households own. Median gross rent is $1,129 and median household income is $54,593. Population is 28,790 for 2025, down from 29,781 in 2020, so buyers have choices and condition matters.

Chapter 1313 of the codified ordinances applies before any sale, transfer or agreement to sell. The buyer must be shown a Certificate of Inspection, or a Certificate of Compliance dated within a year before the agreement. The city's inspection page and the ordinance set out the steps:

  • The owner or an agent applies on the Building Commissioner's form, and the inspection happens within ten days after the application and fee are received.
  • The certificate follows within ten working days after the inspector gains access and lists code violations found, which the owner must correct within 90 days unless the commissioner extends the time for good cause.
  • The fee is $200 for a dwelling and $300 for a commercial building. Each re-inspection after the first two costs $35, and a missed appointment without one business day of notice costs $25.
  • The buyer signs an acknowledgment of receiving the certificate, and a copy goes to the Building Department as a condition of transferring title.
  • If violations remain at closing, escrow of at least $100 and equal to 110 percent of the higher of two written repair estimates is required, or an approved bond.

The ordinance doesn't apply to a transfer by inheritance or gift where no real sale is intended. Escrow agents may not transfer title or release funds until the chapter has been satisfied, so file the application early, before an offer is in hand.

The city requires a notarized Buyer's Acknowledgement Form, returned in original to the office. A business buyer must designate an agent, and an out-of-state business must register with the Ohio Secretary of State as a foreign corporation before the Compliance Certificate is issued.

If the buyer is assuming outstanding violations, a notarized Affidavit is also needed, and the buyer has 90 days from the transfer date to finish the repairs. The seller's signature on the affidavit isn't required for bank-owned, Fannie Mae or Freddie Mac properties. The city also offers separate forms for individuals and businesses, a consent form for an interior inspection, and a snow-covered-property agreement.

The Building and Housing office is at 5407 Turney Road, 2nd floor, open weekdays until 3:45 p.m. Send applications by email to buildingdept@garfieldhts.org or by fax. Emails are processed within two business days, and fees increased in 2025.

sections.h2: Recording and transfer in Cuyahoga County
sections.html:
One Cuyahoga County Fiscal Office division took over what the auditor, recorder and engineer used to do, at 2079 E. Ninth Street, 4th floor, Cleveland. Each transfer must carry a DTE 100 value statement or a DTE 100-EX exemption statement.

Cuyahoga County Fiscal Office, Transfer and Recording
Filing detailWhat to know
Required formDTE 100 or DTE 100-EX
Recording fee$39 for the first two pages, $8 for each additional page, effective October 24, 2024 under Senate Bill 94
Recording closes4:00 p.m. on weekdays
Phone216-443-2060
NotaryDeed signature acknowledged before a notary or similar officer (ORC 5301.01)

Ask the Fiscal Office for the conveyance fee that applies to your sale. Drafting a deed is the practice of law under Ohio Supreme Court rulings, so county staff won't advise you. Owners may draft their own.

sections.h2: Selling a Garfield Heights house with violations
sections.html:
Because of the inspection rule, speed depends on who handles the violations.

  • Agent listing: the buyer sees the certificate up front, and you fix cited items inside 90 days or fund the escrow.
  • Sale as-is to an investor: the buyer can assume violations through the affidavit and finish repairs within 90 days of transfer.
  • Inherited property: a transfer by inheritance or gift without a bona fide sale falls outside the point-of-sale chapter.

The Building and Housing page also links a Cuyahoga County list of homes scheduled for demolition, which requires notice to lien holders first. Ask the department how a long violation list could affect your house.

The Dan Kostel Recreation Center on Turney Road has an outdoor summer pool and an indoor ice rink, and the Garfield Park Reservation, part of Cleveland Metroparks, sits in the northeast corner on the Cleveland border. The Wargo Farms parcel, about 45 acres, was sold to Cleveland Metroparks in 2023 for green space and trails. The Highland Park development, built on a former landfill and bought out of receivership in 2020, has added employers such as MPAC Switchback, MTech, Innoplast and Thermoprene.

The Garfield Heights school system runs three elementary schools, one middle school and Garfield Heights High School. Mention parks and the nearby jobs in a listing, since they answer the first questions buyers ask.

sections.h2: From offer to closing in Garfield Heights
sections.html:
Apply for the inspection as soon as you decide to sell. Once you have a contract, the buyer signs the acknowledgment, the certificate goes to the Building Department, and the title company confirms the chapter has been satisfied. Only then can the escrow agent transfer title or release funds.

The deed goes to the Fiscal Office with a DTE form, and recording follows. Bring photo identification and any mortgage payoff letter to the signing, and the notarized affidavit if the buyer is assuming violations. For a business buyer, check early that its agent is designated and its registration is in order, since the Compliance Certificate waits on both.

A cash buyer will often take a house with open violations, which means the affidavit and the 90-day repair clock rather than an escrow holdback from your proceeds. Ask for each offer in writing, with the price, closing date and who pays each fee, and compare what you net after fees, any tax proration and loan payoff. If you can't tell whether a transfer qualifies as a gift or inheritance, call the Building Department before you sign anything.

faqs.q: Does Garfield Heights make sellers get an inspection first?
faqs.a: Yes. Chapter 1313 ties a sale to a Certificate of Inspection, and the buyer then needs a Compliance Certificate to take title. The dwelling fee is $200 under the 2024 ordinance.

faqs.q: What is the deadline to correct cited violations?
faqs.a: Ninety days from the certificate, unless the Building Commissioner extends it for good cause. A buyer who assumes the violations by affidavit gets 90 days from the transfer date.

faqs.q: Can I sell if I cannot pay for repairs before closing?
faqs.a: Yes, with escrow or a bond. The escrow runs at least $100 and equals 110 percent of the higher of two written estimates. A buyer who signs the affidavit can also take the house with violations open.

faqs.q: Which office files the deed after a Garfield Heights closing?
faqs.a: The Cuyahoga County Fiscal Office, in its Transfer and Recording division at 2079 E. Ninth Street. The deed travels with a DTE 100 or DTE 100-EX, and recording starts at $39 for two pages.

faqs.q: Does an inherited Garfield Heights house skip the inspection?
faqs.a: Only when it passes by inheritance or gift with no real sale intended. Listing the inherited house for sale brings the chapter back into play, so call the Building Department first.
